pack.name: Economics
pack.title: The Invisible Hand Below
pack.blurb: Economists, indicators, taxes, trade and the institutions that steer it all.

prompts.flavor: They promised to explain why we want what we want. The answer was down here all along.
prompts.rules: Any notable economist, living or dead, including central bankers and well-known Australian economists. Surnames alone are fine.

answers.lore: The New Zealander behind the Phillips curve also built the MONIAC in 1949: a machine that modelled the British economy with flowing coloured water.
He worked his passage to Melbourne as a ship's boy in 1855. His single tax on land later inspired the board game that became Monopoly.
Before he helped found modern economics he spent five years in Sydney as an assayer at the Mint, from 1854, and wrote a social survey of the city.

traps.reason: An investor or a business owner rather than an economist.
A politician who ran an economy, which is not quite the same as studying one.
That is the job. Name someone who does it.

prompts.text: Name a winner of the Nobel Prize in economics.
prompts.flavor: Each October a telephone rings in the dark. For a few, the voice on the line speaks Swedish.
prompts.rules: Any laureate of the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, from the first in 1969 to 2026. Surnames alone are fine.

answers.lore: Shared the very first prize, in 1969. He also coined the words econometrics and macroeconomics.
The only Soviet laureate (1975). He invented linear programming in 1939 while helping a plywood factory get more from its machines.

traps.reason: The prize only began in 1969 and is never given to the dead, so this giant missed out.
Famous, and often tipped, but never a laureate.
A Nobel laureate, but not in economics.

prompts.flavor: A room of quiet people decides what money is worth. They never say who they are afraid of.
prompts.rules: Any country's or currency union's central bank or monetary authority, by its name, its initials or simply the country.

aliases: Central Bank of the Russian Federation

answers.answer: Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey

aliases: Banco Central de la República Argentina

answers.answer: Central Bank of the Republic of China

aliases: Central Bank of the United Arab Emirates

answers.answer: Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina
National Bank of the Republic of Belarus
National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic

answers.answer: Bank of the Republic of Burundi
Central Bank of West African States
aliases: Banque Centrale des États de l'Afrique de l'Ouest
Banque des États de l'Afrique Centrale

answers.answer: Central Bank of the Republic of Guinea

aliases: Banco Central de Reserva del Perú

answers.answer: Central Reserve Bank of El Salvador
Bank of the Republic of Haiti
Central Bank of the Dominican Republic
Central Bank of Trinidad and Tobago
Central Bank of Curaçao and Sint Maarten
First Bank of the United States
aliases: Second Bank of the United States

answers.lore: A trick answer that is true: it was Australia's central bank until 1960, when the Reserve Bank was split off from it.
Founded in 1657, it issued Europe's first banknotes in 1661, printed too many, and failed. From its wreck Sweden made the Riksbank, the oldest central bank.

traps.reason: A commercial bank. Name the bank that sets a country's interest rates and issues its money.
An international lender, not a central bank.
Close to the money, but not the central bank.
Which one? Name it, or name its country.

prompts.text: Name a school of economic thought or a type of economic system.
prompts.flavor: Every one of them explains the whole world. The world has declined to comment.
prompts.rules: Any named school, tradition or -ism in economics, or any kind of economic system, such as the one Australia has.

answers.lore: Major C. H. Douglas's 1920s plan to hand every citizen a national dividend. It won government in Alberta in 1935 and spawned parties in Australia and New Zealand.
The Inca Empire fed and housed millions with no money and no markets. Subjects paid tax in labour, the mit'a, and the state stored and shared the produce.

traps.reason: A political system: it says who rules, not how goods are made and shared.
Which one? Give it its name.
A concept every school uses, rather than a school or a system itself.

prompts.text: Name a type of tax or government charge.
prompts.flavor: Two things are certain. The other one, at least, only comes for you once.
prompts.rules: Any kind of tax, duty, levy, excise or tariff, Australian or foreign, current or abolished.

answers.lore: Peter the Great taxed beards from 1698 to make Russians look European. Those who paid carried a token reading: the beard is a superfluous burden.
The emperor Vespasian taxed the urine collected from Rome's public toilets and sold to tanners. Asked if it shamed him, he said: money does not stink.
At first thirty shillings a month to dig, gold or no gold. Hatred of it led to the Eureka Stockade at Ballarat in December 1854.

traps.reason: Which one? Name a particular tax.
Part of the tax system, but not a tax itself.
The collector, not the tax.
A cost of living, perhaps, but not a tax.

prompts.text: Name an economic indicator or statistic.
prompts.flavor: Dials on the bridge of a ship that cannot see the water. Watch the needles. Ignore the knocking below.
prompts.rules: Any measure used to take the pulse of an economy, such as growth, prices, jobs, trade or confidence.

aliases: Balance of trade in goods and services
Real net national disposable income per capita

answers.lore: The future Chinese premier reportedly told a US diplomat in 2007 that he trusted three numbers over GDP: electricity use, rail freight and bank loans.
Alan Greenspan's pet gauge: men put off buying new underwear when money is tight, so a dip in sales hints at trouble ahead.
Andrew Lawrence's 1999 observation that the world's tallest buildings tend to be finished just as a great crash arrives.

traps.reason: A concept or a policy rather than something you can read off a chart each month.
The body that publishes indicators, not an indicator.
Which one? Name the measure.

prompts.text: Name a member of the G20.
prompts.flavor: Twenty chairs around the table, and one more that nobody remembers setting out.
prompts.rules: Any of the nineteen countries and two unions that are full members. Invited guests, even permanent ones, don't count.

answers.lore: The newest member: admitted at the New Delhi summit in September 2023, the first new seat since the group began in 1999.

traps.reason: The permanent guest. Spain is invited to every summit, but it has never been a member.
Not a member, though it may be invited as a guest or sit in through a union.
An organisation, but not one with a seat as a G20 member.

prompts.text: Name an international economic organisation, trade bloc or trade agreement.
prompts.flavor: Treaties signed in rooms with no windows. The ink is dry. Something else is not.
prompts.rules: Any body, bloc, forum or agreement through which countries manage trade, money or development together.

Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development
Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership
General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
Australia New Zealand Closer Economic Relations Trade Agreement
Cairns Group of Fair Trading Nations
United Nations Conference on Trade and Development
South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation
Economic Community of West African States
Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa

answers.answer: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development

aliases: Economic Community of Central African States
West African Economic and Monetary Union
Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries

answers.lore: The customs union Prussia built from 1834. By scrapping tolls between dozens of German states it did much to make one Germany before there was one.
A league of merchant towns that ran Baltic and North Sea trade for 400 years with its own law and fleets, yet never had a king, a seal or a capital.

aliases: Australia-India Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement

traps.reason: A country, not an organisation. Name a body or agreement countries join.
An international body, but its business is security, health, sport or charity rather than the economy.
One country's own institution, not an international one.

prompts.text: Name a country that uses the euro.
prompts.flavor: One coin for many kingdoms. Turn it over and each shows a different face of the same thing.
prompts.rules: Any country whose official currency is the euro: the eurozone members, the microstates, and the two that adopted it on their own.

answers.lore: Not in the EU or the eurozone. It simply switched from the German mark to the euro in 2002, with no say in how the currency is run.
It adopted the euro on its own in 2002, years before declaring independence, and has no seat at the European Central Bank.

traps.reason: It kept the pound, even while it was in the European Union.
Surrounded by the euro, but it still uses the Swiss franc.
A Nordic holdout: it still has its own krona or krone.
In the European Union, but still using its own currency.
In or near Europe, but it has a currency of its own.
That is the whole club. Name one country in it.
Not unless something has gone badly wrong at the Reserve Bank.

prompts.text: Name a cognitive bias, heuristic or effect from behavioural economics.
prompts.flavor: You are certain you chose freely. That certainty is the first item on the list.
prompts.rules: Any named bias, mental shortcut or behavioural effect that bends how people judge and decide.

answers.lore: Franklin won over a rival by asking to borrow a rare book. We grow fonder of people we have done a favour for, to justify having done it.
Given a fine scarlet dressing gown, Denis Diderot replaced his desk, chairs and prints to match it and ended in debt. One purchase begets the next.
The story goes that colonial Delhi paid a bounty for dead cobras, so people bred them. When the bounty ended the snakes were set loose.

traps.reason: Which one? Give the bias its name.
Standard economics, not one of the quirks that behavioural economists study.
A prejudice, and a serious one, but not a named cognitive bias from this field.

prompts.flavor: The holds are full and the hulls ride low. What they carry was in the ground for a billion years.
prompts.rules: Any good or service Australia sells to the world in real quantity, now or in its history.

answers.lore: Australia has the world's largest herd of wild camels, descended from animals imported in the 1800s, and has shipped some back to the Middle East.
Australia invented the polymer banknote in 1988 and has since printed plastic money for dozens of other countries.
Makassan fishermen sailed to Arnhem Land for it from at least the 1700s and traded with Yolngu people: Australia's first export industry.

traps.reason: Protected. Live native animals are not for sale, though zoos do arrange the odd loan.
Australia mostly buys that from overseas: an import, not an export.
Too broad. Name a particular export.
Other way around. Britain exported those to us.

prompts.text: Name a type of good in economics.
prompts.flavor: Everything can be sorted, labelled and priced. Almost everything. Do not ask about the rest.
prompts.rules: Any category economists sort goods and services into, such as the kind people buy less of as they grow richer.

answers.lore: Karl Polanyi's 1944 name for land, labour and money: things bought and sold as if they were made for sale, though none of them was.
Nobel laureate Alvin Roth's term for things many think should never be sold even when buyer and seller agree: kidneys, votes, horse meat in California.

traps.reason: Which kind? Economists have many labels: name one.
That is an example of a good. Name the category an economist would put it in.
A concept, not a type of good.
Not a category, though some shops do make you wonder.

prompts.text: Name a federal Treasurer of Australia.
prompts.flavor: Every one of them stood up on budget night and promised it would all add up. Every one.
prompts.rules: Anyone who has held the office of Treasurer of Australia since 1901, however briefly. Surnames alone are fine.

answers.lore: The first, from 1901. A former Premier of Victoria, he held the purse under Barton, Deakin and Reid.
Treasurer from 1915 to 1916. A Labor man, he resigned when Billy Hughes pushed for conscription.
Treasurer for a few months of 1916 and 1917 in Billy Hughes's breakaway National Labor ministry.

traps.reason: A Prime Minister, but one who never held the Treasury.
Finance Minister: the Treasurer's neighbour, but a different job.
An official of the Reserve Bank or the Treasury department, never the elected Treasurer.
In opposition or in another portfolio, but never Treasurer.
A state Treasurer. The question asks for the federal one.
That is the office. Name someone who held it.

prompts.text: Name a country whose currency is called the dollar.
prompts.flavor: The same word stamped on a hundred different coins. It meant a valley in Bohemia, once.
prompts.rules: Any country or territory whose official money is a dollar of some kind, its own or somebody else's.

answers.lore: Founded by freed American slaves, it named its money the dollar in 1847. Liberian and US dollars still circulate side by side.
The world's smallest republic has never had its own money. It has used the Australian dollar since 1966.
Home to about forty people, most descended from the Bounty mutineers. They use the New Zealand dollar.

traps.reason: Its money has another name: a pound, a euro, a yen, a peso, a rupee or something else again.
That is the currency. Name a country that uses one.
